body:
in Comics/Cartoons, Music |   	October 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Ray Ellis had a six-decade career as a pro­duc­er, arranger, and jazz com­pos­er. And while he’s best known for arrang­ing music for Bil­lie Hol­i­day’s Lady in Satin (1958), he also enjoyed a long career orches­trat­ing music for tele­vi­sion. Work­ing under a pseu­do­nym “Yvette Blais” (his wife’s name), Ellis com­posed back­ground music for the car­toon stu­dio Fil­ma­tion between 1968 and 1982. And, dur­ing the late 60s, he notably cre­at­ed the back­ground and inci­den­tal music for the orig­i­nal Spi­der-Man car­toons.
Above, hear Ray Ellis’ Spi­der-Man sound­track. The show’s talk­ing parts and sound effects have been removed as much as pos­si­ble, then “pieced back togeth­er into com­plete form,” by a YouTu­ber who uses the moniker “11db11.” All of the music from Sea­son 1 is includ­ed, plus many record­ings from Sea­sons 2 and 3. It’s worth not­ing that the 52 episodes from the orig­i­nal 1967 Spi­der-Man TV series have been com­plete­ly restored. You can pur­chase them on DVD online.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

title: Harry Houdini Died 100 Years Ago This Halloween: Was He Really Killed by a Punch to the Stomach?
description:
in History |   	October 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

This Hal­loween marks the 100th anniver­sary of the death of famed escape artist Har­r
body:
in History |   	October 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

This Hal­loween marks the 100th anniver­sary of the death of famed escape artist Har­ry Hou­di­ni. Today, most of us know more about the man­ner of that death than we do about any of the feats of escape artistry that made him famous in the first place. As the sto­ry goes, he’d mas­tered his own body to the extent that he could tight­en his abdom­i­nal mus­cles so as to with­stand even the hard­est punch to the gut. Or at least that’s the image he let cir­cu­late: tak­ing it as a chal­lenge, a stu­dent and ama­teur box­er turned up and offered his fist to Hou­di­ni as an unex­pect­ed test. A week and a half lat­er, the great escapol­o­gist was dead of peri­toni­tis.
It seemed that the blow he sus­tained had rup­tured Hou­dini’s already-inflamed appen­dix, and that remained the wide­ly accept­ed, if not med­ical­ly air­tight, expla­na­tion for near­ly a cen­tu­ry. Yet there was always some­thing too dra­mat­i­cal­ly neat in the tale of a man famed for defy­ing death being done in by noth­ing more than a thought­less young man’s suck­er punch. Gen­er­a­tions of enthu­si­asts have offered expla­na­tions of their own, some more plau­si­ble than oth­ers, but few inves­ti­ga­tions into this qua­si-leg­endary demise have been con­duct­ed as seri­ous­ly as the one under­tak­en in our time by retired urol­o­gist Lar­ri­an Gille­spie, author of Hou­di­ni: The Man Who Died Twice.
When she had the chance to exam­ine his death cer­tifi­cate, Gille­spie noticed appar­ent irreg­u­lar­i­ties that led her down the rab­bit hole to “a paper trail of mis­state­ments and actions by more than a dozen peo­ple close to Hou­di­ni, includ­ing rel­a­tives and employ­ees,” writes the New York Times’ Robin Pogre­bin, “includ­ing a con­spir­a­cy to change his offi­cial death date to Octo­ber 31st, fix­ing his mem­o­ry to Hal­loween.” Accord­ing to her recon­struc­tion of events, Hou­di­ni actu­al­ly died the day before: not of appen­dici­tis, and not as a result of the young man’s punch. “Rather, she argues, the cul­prit was a bow­el obstruc­tion, brought on by a fibrous mass of chop suey that Hou­di­ni ate on Oct. 28.”


	

Emer­gency surgery took place the next day, but it was too late. “Sep­tic shock set in, Houdini’s fever spiked to 105 and his rapid breath­ing led to mus­cle spasms and uncon­scious­ness.” He was oper­at­ed on again the day after, and “Gillespie’s research into the death cer­tifi­cates indi­cates that the magi­cian died that after­noon at 1:26 p.m.” Gille­spie argues that the lack of a prop­er autop­sy helped con­ceal pos­si­ble med­ical mal­prac­tice and allowed Hou­dini’s wid­ow to col­lect a dou­ble-indem­ni­ty pay­ment for what was treat­ed as an acci­den­tal death. Even if accept­ed, her the­o­ry prob­a­bly won’t erase the cul­tur­al link between Hou­di­ni and Hal­loween. But the the­o­ry does add a new dimen­sion of irony to his life sto­ry: the man who could sur­vive a Chi­nese water tor­ture cell proved to be no match for Amer­i­can Chi­nese food.
Relat­ed Con­tent: 
Watch Hou­di­ni Escape From a Strait Jack­et, Then See How He Did It (Cir­ca 1917)

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Artists Take to the Streets Amid Massive Protests in France
description:
Art Week Paris
                Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie in Paris for a march led in part by culture-sector c
body:
Art Week Paris
                Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie in Paris for a march led in part by culture-sector coalitions demanding a better life for artists. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Artists, art students, and cultural workers joined hundreds of thousands of protesters marching across France on October 24, 2026. (photo Nicolas Tucat / AFP via Getty Images)
    
        
            PARIS — On the heels of last Saturday’s mass protests — and amid the preemptive closure of Art Basel Paris and museums like the Louvre — Paris’s artists, culture workers, and art students were back in the streets today, October 24. Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie for a march called in part by Cultures en Lutte, the network of culture-sector coalitions that has mobilized alongside the labor confederations and student unions since the movement began in mid-September, and by one of its driving forces, the National Union of Visual Artists (SNAP-CGT).  They came despite a week of warnings. After the destruction of October 17, the French government announced a “massive” security deployment: Sentinelle anti-terror soldiers would relieve police of guard duties, while special units would be backed by helicopters, armored vehicles, and water cannons. More than 250,000 protestors turned out anyway in Paris, and several hundred thousand more around the country, reports estimate. Police arrested approximately 1,000 protesters just today.  A painted sign depicts French President Emmanuel Macron using "our rights" as toilet paper.Students pose with their signs at the October 24 protest. The left sign warns against the use of AI; the right sign reads, “The boat is sinking, but the politicians are fighting over who will be captain.”

title: This Is Class War
description:
Weekly Newsletter
                The latest on the student protests in France, the art world’s AI problem, one-on-one with Rosa
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                The latest on the student protests in France, the art world’s AI problem, one-on-one with Rosana Paulino, and Beer With a Painter featuring Melissa Brown.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            The subway car rattles, shakes, and screeches as it tunnels us from Brooklyn to Manhattan underneath the East River. I hold on tight to a pole, while my eyes are fixed on an ad for the Broadway musical Les Misérables. My social media feed shows me only looting and vandalism in France, painting a violent picture of the largely peaceful student protests. Panicking, the art world’s blue-chip class shuts down Art Basel Paris early and flees the city. The Louvre also closes to protect its treasures. Loot a little and they throw you in jail; loot a lot and they let you open a museum. I get to a benefit dinner for an art residency held in a former bank. A peppy auctioneer asks the who’s who to open their hearts and wallets. Paddles go up and down, and a donation ticker on a big screen climbs to astronomical numbers while I admire the building’s huge stained-glass skylight. Up there, near a golden clock that no longer ticks, an inscription in marble letters reads, "It's what we save rather than what we earn that ensures a competence for the future."Outside, Midtown Manhattan is huffing and puffing, and the neon lights glow too bright. A sign in a bodega window advertises that the Powerball jackpot has hit $650 million, and I drift into a daydream about what my life would be like if I won that much money. I picture myself raising the paddle at auctions and amassing a serious art collection — just to support artists, you know. I sit somewhere for a coffee and see the barista trying to buy a ticket on her phone for a new movie about white-collar convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes, who’s become a cultural icon among the petite bourgeoisie. The barista can’t find a ticket because the theater is sold out.  On the subway ride back home, I get sucked into an essay about Kazimir Malevich’s concept of the “White Abyss” and miss my stop by several stations, adding an hour to my commute. I get off in an impoverished neighborhood and see that someone has graffitied “Class War” all over a residential building. There’s nothing open but a convenience store at a gas station. Fuck it, I’m buying a Powerball ticket.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			Dear Art World, We Can Tell When You’re Using AI
		
	
	
		Wall labels. Press releases. Artist statements. In today’s fast-paced art world, the written word stands at a crucial crossroads — and the stakes have never been higher. But here’s the thing: It’s not just about convenience. It’s about authenticity. Because the way we express ourselves matters.

The above paragraph was generated by Claude when prompted to write an introduction for an opinion piece against AI use in art writing, and if it made you recoil in your seat, you may be among those of us who have developed a strong aversion to generative text. You’ll know it when you see it: that uncanny cadence that’s overconfident in style yet hollow in substance, like a motivational LinkedIn post that feels relatable at first but leaves you with as much nourishment as a spoonful of Stevia. | Valentina Di Liscia

Escher and Marc Chagall.

far-right president removes works referencing LGBTQ+ and women’s rights and political violence.As negotiations continue at the Victoria & Albert Museum, unionized staff are set to strike across all the protests and the surreal experience of attending Paris Art Week while smelling burning plastic.French student demonstrators are upending the country’s public landmarks to denounce police violence, under-resourced schools, and a worsening cost-of-living crisis — much like the protests of 1968.Dozens of students from the École du Louvre in Paris block the main entrance of the Louvre Museum title: 50 Artworks by Artists Who Lived and Worked in India Gifted to the Tate
description: 50 artworks from the collection of Charles Greig, a British academic and expert in Indian art, have been donated to the Tate. The collection include
body:
50 artworks from the collection of Charles Greig, a British academic and expert in Indian art, have been donated to the Tate. The collection includes oil paintings, watercolors and miniatures by artists who lived and worked in India during the 18th and 19th centuries.

	The museum described the gift as an “entirely philanthropic act,” with Greig donating the works outright and without the use of tax incentives. Greig built the collection over four decades and features artists such as Sita Ram and Ghulam Ali Khan—who capitalized on the new market for their work among British East India Company officials—as well as European artists such as Johan Zoffany and Rudolf Swoboda, and British landscapists like William Hodges, Thomas Daniell and William Daniell. The works in the collection reflect India and Britain’s shared history and complex power dynamics between the two nations.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Greig said in a statement that the main focus of his collection was an exploration of the “deep and intricate relationship between Britain and the Indian subcontinent through the entwined complexities of the artistic encounter. Most of the works were made in the vanished world before photography and they provide us with a visual record of our rich shared history from about 1770.” He called assembling this collection his life’s “primary passion, but at no stage did I ever see myself as other than a temporary steward.”

	Notable artworks in the collection include German painter Johan Zoffany’s Portrait of Prince Jawan Bakht (also known as Jahandar Shah) (1784), making it one of only three portraits of individual Indian sitters by the artist to be held in UK public collections; Austrian painter Rudolph Swoboda’s Sepoy in HH Maharaja Srinagar’s Indian Regiment, 23 Years Old (1886), painted for Queen Victoria, is the first work by the artist to enter a British museum collection. The three watercolors by Sita Ram draw on  both Indian art traditions and European visual languages. 

	“These works encompass a unique cross-cultural discourse, it seems to me vital that they are preserved intact to be enjoyed and studied by all mankind. A collection built on a life of study deserves to be universally accessible and I am profoundly happy to see these works find a permanent home at Tate,” said Greig.
	

	The collection is expected to be exhibited at the Tate Britain in 2028. Alex Farquharson, director of Tate Britain, said in a statement that the museum is “always looking to tell new and different stories about Britain’s role in international art history” and that this gift from Greig will “significantly strengthen our holdings of art produced in the British Empire and broaden the range of people and histories represented in the national collection.”

title: In a Historic Blunder, Wu-Tang Clan Sold an Album as a Unique Artwork—A New Doc Tells the Story of an Architect of the Sale
description: If you were on the internet in 2015, you likely followed the twisty tale of the Wu-Tang Clan‘s Once Upon a Time in Shaolin. The Staten Island hip-ho
body:
If you were on the internet in 2015, you likely followed the twisty tale of the Wu-Tang Clan‘s Once Upon a Time in Shaolin. The Staten Island hip-hop titans conceived of the album as a conceptual artwork, a protest against the cheapening of music in the age of widespread piracy. Rather than release the music to the general public, the work was sold at auction for a reported $2 million to a then-anonymous American buyer, seemingly proving that music could sell at the level of Picasso and Warhol.

	It proved a Pyrrhic victory when the buyer was revealed to be the hated “pharma bro” Martin Shkreli. The episode was a bitter lesson for the group, resulting in resentment and division. Even Clan member Method Man said, “Fuck that album. … When music can’t be music and y’all turning it into something else, fuck that. Give it to the people, if they want to hear the shit, let them have it. Give it away free.” (He somewhat softened his stance recently, on finally hearing the album.)
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	A new Netflix documentary, The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable (2026), presents a long and shaggy ride through the experience. Directed by producer Joanna Natasegara and featuring RZA as an executive producer, the film proves a frustrating watch: no one involved seems to, even now, have thought much about the lessons from their attempt to hijack the art market, a sometimes unpredictable world they blundered into, seeming to know little about it while somehow assuming that’s where the big money was. “Contemporary art is worth millions by virtue of its exclusivity,” said the band at the time. Of course, a vanishingly small percentage of artworks of any era are priced at that level, but maybe their misconception is understandable, since the members’ art world reference points, at least judging by the way they are quoted in the film, seem to be restricted to Leonardo da Vinci, Picasso, and Warhol.

	Many of the art world’s denizens could have warned them away from the stunt. Funnily enough, in 2017, during the whole dustup, Richard Prince disavowed an artwork he had sold to Ivanka Trump before her father’s entry into politics. Of course, by then it was too late to warn RZA.

	The album’s sale is mentioned in the opening sequence, with audio of an unidentified interviewer calling it “one of the coolest stories in art history.” RZA explains the thinking: “We’ll make one single copy of the album, treat it like it’s the Mona Lisa. It was a combination of ideas that led to it. Me and my student Cilvaringz—won’t take all the credit.”
	

	“Would you ever do it again?” asks the interviewer.

	Says the rapper, in a loaded two-letter word, “Um …”
	
		The Shaggy Tale of an Unfolding Mess	

	The film then doesn’t mention the album again for a full 55 minutes, instead plunging the viewer at great length into the life story of Dutch-Moroccan rapper-producer Tarik Azzougarh, one of the masterminds of the project, including his traumatic childhood experiences of racism and abuse.

	The director found him compelling, she explains in press materials: “Over a long lunch in beautiful Marrakech, where he lived, Tarik told me the twists and turns of the album’s 30-year story, and I was fascinated. It wasn’t only a great story; it resonated with me personally as someone who grew up in the ’90s with mixed heritage. The Wu-Tang Clan often talk about being teenagers inspired by East Asian culture through movies, while Tarik and his friends had, in turn, been inspired by the Clan.”


			
			
			
	
			
					Tarik Azzougarh in The Disciple. 
									Courtesy of Netflix © 2026
	



	Unfortunately, for my money, Azzougarh doesn’t ultimately prove a compelling presence on screen. “I figured that a doc would show my side of the story,” Azzougarh tells the off-camera director early on, in a characteristically not-quite-electrifying observation.

	The film slowly relates that the aspiring rapper and superfan ingratiated himself into the band’s circles, flying to New York multiple times as a teenager for the purpose. He earned the sobriquet Cilvaringz and membership in the Killa Beez, a network of musicians in the extended Wu-Tang family, releasing his own records on their imprint as well as producing some of the Clan’s albums.
	

	Once Upon a Time was packaged in a custom handcrafted silver box and traveled with all the pomp and security of a seven-figure artwork, as the film shows. Only one copy will ever legally exist, in a protest against the loss of music’s aura in the age of its digital reproducibility, to paraphrase German philosopher Walter Benjamin. The band sold the record via online auctioneer Paddle8 in 2015, with the stipulation that the buyer could not release it commercially for 88 years, though they could play it at listening parties.


			
			
			
	
			
					Wu-Tang’s 2015 album Once Upon a Time in Shaolin.
									Courtesy of Netflix © 2026
	



	In keeping with the fine art theme, the band staged a listening event at MoMA PS1, after which Complex described the record as “rich, layered, and sonically bombastic,” with a “rugged, hard-hitting sound” reminiscent of early Wu-Tang Clan albums. Writing for ARTnews, a slightly more skeptical Dan Duray noted, “There were plenty of unexpected samples, melodramatic horns, cheesy bits of kung-fu dialogue.” Snippets are audible in the documentary.

	Then Shkreli was arrested, and some of the film’s funnier moments come with the discussion of Wu-Tang’s attempts to find a way to reverse the sale and get the music to the people, including a rumored clause in the contract by which either Clan members or actor Bill Murray could legally steal the record back.
	

	In 2018, Shkreli was convicted of securities fraud and conspiracy, and the Department of Justice sold the record to help pay his reparations. In 2021, it sold, for some $4 million, to digital art and crypto collective PleasrDAO, in whose hands it remains today. The group’s late founder, Jamis Johnson, said in 2021 that “there’s not a world in which we don’t own this album.” The group has organized several listening events, at venues from the Museum of Old and New Art in Tasmania to the Angel Orensanz Center, housed in a 175-year-old former synagogue in New York.


			
			
			
	
			
					Silversmith Yahya, right, in The Disciple. 
									Courtesy of Netflix © 2026
	



	So now Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, with all its contradictions and challenges, is PleasrDAO’s problem. In a video interview with ARTnews, the collective’s “chief pleasing officer,” Jamis’s brother Adrian Johnson, outlined the tricky position in which the group finds itself.

	“We don’t want the record to be streamed,” he said. “The moment it is, it becomes another album.”

	He went on, “Everything about it is a paradox: it’s for the people, but it’s also highly guarded. It’s quite a difficult job as stewards of this art to say, ‘How can we bring it to the people but not devalue it?,’ and I don’t believe that keeping it locked away is right. I also don’t believe making it freely available is right. So we are constantly looking for creative ways to share this with the people.”
	

	For future activations, keep an eye on a dedicated website, and tune in to Netflix for the documentary, but don’t hold out for too much excitement. I give it a passing grade.

title: Walid Raad’s Way of Working Is Inspired by the Mirrors in Vampire Movies
description: As a teenager, Walid Raad would walk around his hometown with a camera, just trying to make some sense of the world. At a glance, the black-and-whit
body:
As a teenager, Walid Raad would walk around his hometown with a camera, just trying to make some sense of the world. At a glance, the black-and-white pictures he captured then offer cool, detached views. But he quickly discovered there was only so much sense to be made of war-torn Beirut. One day, walking by a bakery, he snapped a cake displayed in the window. It was decorated with birthday wishes for someone named Hassan. Only later, developing the film at home—his dad had converted the bathroom to a darkroom, encouraging his hobby—did Raad register the date: The cake was for Hassan Nasrallah, then a rising militiaman in the Lebanese Civil War. Raad briefly fantasized about poisoning it. “But I was 15,” he told me, laughing. “I was a coward.”
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Decades later, with a PhD and a MoMA retrospective under his belt, Raad returned to that image in a series of digitally fabricated birthday cakes addressed to political leaders who feel difficult to celebrate: happy birthday to Ali, Kamal, Tony, Walid; joyeux anniversaire to Yasser, Elias, Nabih, Amine. By then, Nasrallah had become the leader of Hezbollah; in 2024, he was killed in an Israeli airstrike. Raad’s colorful cakes are at once cheerful and cold—his trademark tragicomic blend of fiction and fact. In his cakes, as in so much of his work, grand political events unfold on an intimate, human scale.

	Begun, in a sense, when Raad was just 15, the cake project has everything of his signature: He starts with something true—a document—then extrapolates its logic to create something fictional, maybe even a little fantastical. That method has carried him through a nearly 40-year career and counting.


			
			
			
	
			
					Walid Raad/The Atlas Group: Festival of Gratitude, 2003/2021.
									Courtesy Paula Cooper Gallery, New York/©Walid Raad; Opposite: Photo Steven Probert Studio/Courtesy Paula Cooper Gallery, New York/©Walid Raad
	



	His work is a standout in the main show in this year’s Venice Biennale: His paintings, drawings, and photographs of banal-seeming beds spring to life when you read a wall text claiming that they were slept in by Yasser Arafat, who “is said to have never slept in the same bed two nights in a row.” The PLO leader survived more than 40 assassination attempts, and “he could not afford to throw caution to the wind… so he lived—and slept—on the move.” Raad adds that he has spent 30 years searching for the beds Arafat slept in, drafting paintings of his mattresses and duvets that he just couldn’t seem to complete.
	

	With the beds and cakes alike, the story unfolds quite literally along the images’ edges: The paintings of the beds are incomplete, bordered with tape and brushstrokes. The birthday cakes appear pulled out of manila envelopes along with piles of pictures, as if being entered into evidence at a trial. Raad says he is “creating the documents I wished already existed.”


			
			
			
	
			
					Walid Raad: Far from quieting_Tunis, 1969–2026.
									Courtesy Paula Cooper Gallery, New York/©Walid Raad
	



	SINGLING OUT RAAD’S Arafat pictures in the Biennale, the scholar Saidiya Hartman described his “belief in the imaginative and the speculative” as “critical.” Hartman has devoted her life’s work to imagining the lives of oppressed people who left limited traces in the archive—people who were silenced or illiterate, people whose voices were only recorded under conditions of coercion, or people who necessarily lived clandestine lives—like Arafat. She calls her approach “critical fabulation.”

	Indeed, Raad is best known for his own method of fabulation, marrying stories and pictures, imaginations and histories. This way of working has everything to do with his primary subject: the Arab world and its politics and conflicts—particularly the Lebanese Civil War (1975—90) that unfolded in Raad’s youth. While floods of images and their competing narratives have all but defined the digital age, this battleground of misinformation has had notable consequences in the region. “During the war,” remembers Khalil Joreige, another Lebanese artist exhibiting in the Venice Biennale this year, “every militia had its own media station, television, newspaper, or radio. There was a real war of images”—a war Joreige says influenced his generation’s “sophisticated relationship to images.”
	

	Accordingly, the Harvard art historian Carrie Lambert-Beatty has described Raad’s work as an exemplar of “parafiction,” adding that one of the most powerful things art can do is get viewers to experience a given scenario as having been true—and remind them that other worlds are possible. In her recent book on artistic research, art historian Claire Bishop singled out Raad too, noting that, while so much work in the genre reproduces the experience of information overload—think: documents in vitrines—Raad offers synthesis in the form of narrative, all without collapsing into the trope of authoritative master narratives against which so much research-based art reacts.

	In my own book, Fables & Forensics, I describe Raad’s work as a kind of surrealism for the information age, noting how he gives playful form to the ordinary if dizzying glut of misinformation—but adding that he does so without ever falling into the trap of reproducing fake news. Any fact—a bed, or a birthday cake—that could be mistaken for true is of little consequence, and there are always clues as to the constructed nature of his documents; just remember to look at the edges.


			
			
			
	
			
					View of Raad’s installation Postscript to the Arabic Edition, 1938–2025, in the 61st Venice Biennale.
									Photos Marco Zorzanello/Courtesy Venice Biennale
	



	Raad is best known for the work he made as a fictional collective called the Atlas Group, work that presses on photography’s fraught relationship with truth. The Group’s video Hostage: The Bachar tapes (#17 and #31), which they attribute to the year 2000, sees Souheil Bachar narrate his experience of being held hostage in Lebanon from 1983 to ’93 alongside five Western men; he was the only Arab. Some scenes simply show Bachar against a white wall, though the video reveals itself as obviously manipulated by way of green-screened footage of Ronald Reagan. There are less obvious clues, too: If you don’t speak Arabic, you might miss how Bachar’s words are at times contradicted by the English translation.
	

	The Group, Raad says, ran from 1989 to 2004. But dates, like all facts, are his medium. You’ll also find magazines and museums that trace the Group’s origin to 1967, the year of Raad’s birth, or to 1948, or 1945. And the Group has attributed archival images to nonexistent institutions—like the Museum of Fine Art New York. Both the Tate and the Museum of Modern Art in New York have acquired editions of his series “My Neck Is Thinner than a Hair: Engines,” but each lists the work with different dates (2000—03 and 1996—2004, respectively). And though Raad says he discontinued the Atlas Group in 2004, a work from the Group appears in the 2026 Venice Biennale catalog, with the date “printed 2023”—leaving it ambiguous as to when it was made, and whether the Group has really disbanded at all.


			
			
			
	
			
					Walid Raad/The Atlas Group: Let’s be honest, the weather helped_Saudi Arabia, 1998.
									Courtesy Paula Cooper Gallery, New York/©Walid Raad
	



	Still, one date is clear: Over the past two decades—since a 2005 catalyst—Raad’s work has only grown stranger. The Atlas Group primed viewers to read his documents as unstable, but the later work asks them to contend with shrunken objects, resurrected paintings, and vampires lurking in the archive. Something has shifted, and the old language of fact and fiction only scratches the surface.
	

	IN A RESTORED 19th-century barn perched on a peak in the so-called “Irish Alps” in upstate New York, Raad keeps a meticulous archive. About an hour’s drive from Bard College, where he teaches, he and his wife duplicated the barn’s floor plan to build a second structure nearby: their home. The view from their porch is straight out of a Hudson River School painting, and meeting him for the first time feels like a peek behind the curtain: For over 20 years, he has diligently hidden his likeness from all corners of the internet, populating the algorithm with other faces to throw it off his scent. He explained his evasiveness in one word—“phobia”—but it was hard not to see it as just one more way Raad uses photography to make the world feel larger and stranger, rather than to try to “capture” it. In person, he is warm and welcoming, serving homemade tabbouleh and hummus “the right way”—with sumac and olive oil.

	In the barn, Raad has assiduously organized ephemeral materials like wall labels from his exhibitions and name cards from dinners he’s attended, all fodder that may or may not become an artwork in the future. A strappy leather portfolio contained his juvenilia, including those pictures he made as a teenager. He went to high school in Boston—“They had a darkroom and they had a basketball team, so it was great,” he said—where he made pictures in the style of Cindy Sherman, Diane Arbus, Garry Winogrand, Stephen Shore, Henri Cartier-Bresson, and Lucas Samaras. Raad was able to approximate all of their styles, but what he carried from the exercise most clearly was the experience of embodying a persona from behind the camera.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					A 2026 self-portrait by Walid Raad.
									Courtesy Paula Cooper Gallery, New York/©Walid Raad
	



	In 1985, Raad started his undergraduate degree at the Rochester Institute of Technology, where he majored in medicine before switching to photography. While there, he won his first photography prize, for a work he made under the pseudonym P.X. Chesterfield, inspired by a real US Marine Corps general, P.X. Kelley, whose name he thought sounded cool. Soon after, he enrolled in the University of Rochester’s “Cultural and Visual Studies” PhD program, which sported rising-star faculty: Craig Owens, Kaja Silverman, Douglas Crimp. It “was psychoanalysis, linguistics, and Marxism,” Raad explained. “The holy trinity.” For Raad, persona, theory, and photography were starting to converge.

	As a student, Raad visited and photographed Beirut each summer, a practice he continues to this day. Back home, he tried aping observational techniques from Diane Arbus or Eugène Atget that he’d observed in photography magazines his dad gave him. But he found that “even something as simple as using a tripod was impossible… in a city that’s full of snipers.” He wasn’t making war photography, either, never capturing the actions, always the aftermath.

	After taking pictures of detonated bombs, however, Raad was often left with the sense that something was missing, so he started getting his hands on the pictures—circling detritus with a red pencil. Kernels of his most famous works are palpable in his teenage years, which seems appropriate for an artist who describes himself as starting out with an interest in “a certain way of thinking about violence and trauma.” Versions of those red circles recur in the Atlas Group’s Let’s Be Honest, the Weather Helped (1998/2006), black-and-white snapshots of Beirut marked with brightly colored dots corresponding to the code system that ammunition manufacturers use to identify cartridges and shells—and thus, indirectly, their makers. In Raad’s hands, the dots read as much confetti as forensic notations.
	

	Under the Atlas Group, Raad was crafting personas like the gambling historian Dr. Fadl Fakhouri and the unlucky police detective Yussef Bitar—“very serious, very professional people,” he explained—the kind likely to leave behind official documents. But eventually, he found the Atlas Group “somewhat limited,” and became interested in showing how “violence has more insidious effects than we know.” Besides, he added, by the early aughts, he felt that “the language of maps and archives had been exhausted.”

	RAAD’S THINKING BEGAN to shift after meeting, in the early ’90s, the Lebanese writer and artist Jalal Toufic while working on a video project about the occupation of South Lebanon. He started reading Toufic’s books, which he found difficult to parse at first, but eventually, he found Forthcoming (2000). That book includes the story of a classically trained photographer who can’t stop making blurry pictures of buildings in Beirut. Raad instantly recognized himself.

	“I freaked out,” Raad told me. “It was as if he could hear my internal monologue.” He thought about how certain photographic tropes—something as simple as a tripod—had been rendered unavailable to him in wartime Beirut, but soon was thinking more expansively about all that violence had withdrawn from him. His trinity-training in Rochester had taught him that “language, psyche, the economy… that’s the stuff of the world.” Toufic, he said, gave him language for “a different place that I’d never been introduced to.”
	

	Toufic has influenced almost everything Raad has made since that encounter. “I’m embarrassed by how much I talk about that guy,” he told me. “It’s as if I cannot have a thought without passing through him.” Of lasting impact was Toufic’s concept of “withdrawal,” spelled out most explicitly in The Withdrawal of Tradition Past a Surpassing Disaster (2009) but also addressed in earlier essays. In it, he describes the sorts of immaterial losses that can arise in the wake of major cultural upheavals—the ways that rituals and forms can become unavailable or lose their potency when the society that gave rise to them is changed irreversibly by disaster.

	Tradition, Toufic theorizes, might be clung to steadfastly in the aftermath of disaster, as in the revival of Orthodox Judaism in the wake of the Holocaust; or it might be suppressed entirely, as in versions of modernism that, also in the wake of the world wars, try in vain to imagine a clean slate and abolish antecedents. When a tradition comes back to life in a new context, something is always off: Toufic calls the act a “resurrection,” because the tradition is not alive so much as undead. The artist’s job is to make this withdrawal palpable—to make the absence present, “like the mirror in vampire films”; for Toufic, only those who try and fail to resurrect withdrawn tradition “may become truly absolutely modern.”
	

	This concept of withdrawal informed the pivotal work Raad showed at the Arab world’s first white cube gallery, Sfeir-Semler Gallery, which opened in 2005. He’d declined the invitation several times before eventually acquiescing in 2008, sensing that something seemed off. When he arrived at the gallery, he found that the Atlas Group’s work he shipped had been shrunk to 1/100th of its original size. When I pressed Raad on how this could be possible, he said that “there are conditions under which your own work is no longer available to you, and your only relation to it feels distorted.” For him, this is not “a symptom, and not a metaphor.” It’s also “not quantum,” nor a condition of “one’s psyche, material conditions, or language”—it is, he said, “withdrawal.” Withdrawal is also the very reason he could not complete those Arafat bed paintings.

	The affinities between Raad and Toufic are striking enough that more than one person has confessed their suspicion that Toufic is simply another of Raad’s personas—a theory that would require an elaborate ruse if true, with Raad hiring a body double to appear alongside him at public events. But while Raad is undoubtedly skilled at crafting fictions and personas, he is less interested in pranks than in fables—in what happens when something is imagined as having been true rather than in trickery and illusion.
	


			
			
			
	
			
									Courtesy Paula Cooper Gallery, New York/©Walid Raad
	



	AFTER THE ATLAS GROUP mined the archive and rendered it strange, Raad’s work went beyond scrambling fact and fiction and toward something more like magical realism. Along the way, photography—which is so hard to read without thinking about truth—became less central. Better be watching the clouds again and again (2000/2017) is a series of collages attributed to a fictional Lebanese Army officer named Fadwa Hassoun, who’d trained as a botanist. During the war, Hassoun assigned politicians flowers as code names, and the work that tells her story features black-and-white portraits of Benjamin Netanyahu, Saddam Hussein, Ronald Reagan, and more with their heads crowned by colorful petals, their legs made to look like stems.

	More recently, Raad collaborated with graphic designer Pierre Huyghebaert on I thought I’d escape my fate (again) (2025), an installation that gathers statements from people involved in exhibitions and programs canceled over expressions of solidarity with Palestine. Printed, cut out, and taped low along a gallery baseboard, these quotes are hard to read without crouching. What catches the eye instead are the colored strips of tape running across the wall, like placeholders for the artworks that never got to hang in such a space. It’s another example of how disaster can show up in art sideways, of Toufic’s idea that conflict leaves traces that are visible in artworks and cultural traditions only in the form of absence—that a “truly modern” artwork might make this absence visible.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Walid Raad (in collaboration with Pierre Huyghebaert): I thought I’d escape my fate (again), 2025; in “we refuse_d,” 2025–26, at Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art, Doha.
									Courtesy Paula Cooper Gallery, New York, and Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art, Doha/©Walid Raad
	



	Toufic’s vampire-mirror idea resurfaces too in other works of Raad’s on display in Venice, alongside the Arafat pieces. Copies of stolen Arab and Turkish artworks appear painted on the undersides of wooden pallets. Here, as in several recent works, the vampire Raad holds a mirror up to is modern Arab art itself, which lately has undergone a period of “rediscovery,” to use the art world’s favorite term—or, resurrection. When the Lebanese Civil War ended in 1990, a wall text informs, militias sold off weapons, many of which found their way to the Balkans; the Yugoslav Wars, then, were fought partly with Lebanese arms. The text adds that the painted pallets were recently found in Ljubljana, at the Moderna Galerija—where, conveniently, he just closed a mid-career retrospective.

	Next spring, at Paula Cooper Gallery in New York, Raad will place a vintage VW Beetle on its back in the gallery like a dying bug—a reference to “flying Volkswagens,” as American soldiers called the artillery shells they fired on Beirut in the 1980s. Surrounding them on the walls will be reproductions of handwritten notes left on bombs by soldiers in various languages, including English, Russian, Arabic, Hebrew, and French—like xoxo, or the dildo of consequences rarely arrives lubed, or from silicon valley with love. Raad found images on Reddit posted by braggadocious soldiers from around the world, and then exaggerated the size and changed the color of their inscriptions. There isn’t a whole lot of fiction or fantasy in this one: Sometimes, the facts are strange enough.

schema.headline: Walid Raad’s Way of Working Is Inspired by the Mirrors in Vampire Movies
